To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) facial attributes such as gender and race are highly correlated with facial appearance and (ii) commercial computer vision classifiers are affected by the facial attributes of the input image.

(i) gender and race cues in facial images affect computer vision classifiers’ predictions; (ii) the effects are different across classifiers; (iii) the effects are more pronounced for facial attributes such as age and hair color than for facial attributes such gender and race; (iv) the effects vary across concepts.

the question of how to evaluate the fairness of a model in the context of computer vision, and how to measure the impact of gender and racial cues in the images on model predictions.

the fairness of commercial face recognition systems is highly dependent on gender and race.

The main takeaway from our work is that

gender and race cues in facial images are indeed important signals for computer vision systems and the extent to which these systems are affected by these cues can be measured using our proposed framework.
gender is a strong predictor of the fairness of computer vision models.
gender and race biases in computer vision models are not always due to inherent biases in the model, but can be due to biases in the training data.
